title: A letter
tomorrow: what did Jesus tell worried people to go and stare at?

cards: Open a drawer in an old family house and there may be a bundle of letters tied with string. The bills got thrown out long ago.
What stayed are the notes that said something kind and specific, in a handwriting someone would know anywhere. That's yesterday's question answered: nobody throws away the letter that saw them.
The New Testament keeps letters too, and some of their best lines are just names.

teach.b: Paul's letter to the Romans ends with a long run of greetings. Two of them, in the King James Bible: “Salute Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.”
Salute means greet. These are people we'd never know about otherwise, remembered because someone noticed their work and wrote it down. Not great job, everyone: names, and what each one did.
The opposite of a form letter. To another church Paul turns it into a habit for everybody: “Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.”
Edify means build up, the way you'd build a house.
And the letter to the Hebrews uses a word you might not expect: “And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works.” Provoke, in the good direction.
A weekly note does exactly this: one person, one specific thing you've seen in them, written down.
It sits easily beside the rest of the week, the gathering, the rest, the friends, the fast, the table.

how: Some Christians write a short note of encouragement each week, to a friend, a family member or someone in their church, often naming one specific thing they're grateful for in that person.

o: a formal complaint sent to a church leader
a short weekly note that builds someone up
a long letter that explains church teaching

games.q: the week's lines — tap the pairs.
p: unto love and to good works

s: encouragement in Paul's letters mostly means telling people to cheer up
it means building up, and Romans does it by naming people and their labor.
Paul's letter to the Romans ends with greetings to people by name
Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis are among them, each named with their labor.
in Hebrews, provoke is only used in a bad sense
let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works.

games.q: at the end of the season, your coach texts the team "great job, everyone!" one player quietly drove the younger kids home all year. what would the end of Romans do?
o: name her, and what she did.
keep it general so nobody feels left out.
praise the whole team again, louder.
games.why: Romans 16 greets people by name with their work: Tryphena and Tryphosa, who labour in the Lord; Persis, which laboured much.

practice: With a pen, write one person's name at the top of a scrap of paper, and under it one specific thing you've seen them do. Not great job; the thing itself, the way Paul wrote about Persis.
Fold it once, and it's ready to send: a card, a text, or a note left on a pillow, whichever that person would actually keep.

wordCard.voice: A letter. A weekly note that names a person and the good you've seen, the kind that ends up tied with string.
